title: Meta-Optimization of Heuristics (MoH): Learning to Build Better Solvers
one_liner: Instead of hard-coding a fixed optimizer, use an LLM to learn how to build better optimizers that discover solutions to hard puzzles.
lead: Hard puzzles (traveling salesman, bin packing, routing) need smart search strategies. Usually you hand-code one optimizer and train it. MoH flips this: it trains an LLM to write its own optimizer code, then uses that optimizer to solve puzzles. The LLM learns which strategies work best across many puzzle types, so it builds an optimizer that generalizes far better than one you designed by hand.

problem.h2: The old way: hand-coded optimizers trap you
paras: To solve a hard puzzle like the traveling salesman problem (TSP), you write an optimizer: a step-by-step search recipe. The recipe might be crossover one solution with another, then mutate parts randomly. But this fixed recipe limits what strategies the system can discover.

A beginner might try: write one optimizer, train it on TSP instances of size 20. It learns to solve those. But when you give it size 200, it fails completely, because the strategy that works on tiny puzzles does not scale. You need a new optimizer for each problem size, or each problem type. And there are infinitely many problems.
The deeper trap: you chose the recipe (crossover then mutate). You are blind to strategies you did not think of. So even on familiar puzzles, your optimizer is stuck in the box you built.

callout.html: Let an LLM learn to write optimizer code itself, training on many puzzle types at once, so it discovers strategies that work across all of them.

panels.title: 1. The locked optimizer
panels.caption: You hand-code a single fixed optimizer recipe for all puzzles.

panels.title: 2. It fails on new problems
panels.caption: That recipe works on training puzzles, collapses on new sizes or types.

panels.title: 3. MoH writes optimizer code
panels.caption: LLM generates optimizer code, prompted with problem details and past working strategies.

panels.title: 4. Multi-task meta-learning
panels.caption: Train the LLM on many problem types at once, so it learns universal strategies.

panels.title: 5. It generalizes everywhere
panels.caption: The learned meta-optimizer works on sizes and problems it never saw.

steps.text: You show the LLM details about TSP or bin packing, plus a library of heuristics that worked before.
It generates text code: a custom search recipe (e.g., a different flavor of selection or mutation) tailored to this puzzle.
The new optimizer code runs on the puzzle, proposing and refining candidate solutions.
Measure how good the solutions are. The score tells you if the new optimizer code was smart.
Feed the score back to the LLM. After many trials across many puzzle types, it learns which ideas generalizes.

paras: Instead of starting with a fixed, hand-coded optimizer, the paper changes the entire level of the game: it makes the LLM learn to generate optimizer code itself. The LLM becomes a meta-optimizer (optimizer-maker), not just a heuristic-maker. This is one level up.

hidden.h2: Cross-problem generalization: solving new puzzle sizes
hidden.name: Generalization gap (old size vs. new size)
paras: The hidden quantity is not a number inside the algorithm; it is a property you measure: how much does the optimizer degrade when you give it a puzzle size or type it never trained on? On size 20, the hand-coded optimizer gets 90% accuracy. On size 200, it drops to 30%. That 60-point gap is the generalization failure.

MoH addresses this by training on many sizes and types at once. The LLM learns which features of a strategy make it work across sizes: ideas that scale up (still find good solutions on size 200) versus ideas that only work on tiny puzzles. A strategy that works on sizes 20, 50, and 100 will likely work on 200, because the LLM picked up universal principles rather than size-specific tricks.

heat.caption: Darker: more effective at generalizing across sizes. Hybrid and learned strategies (top) beat fixed hand-coded ones (bottom).

reads.html: When you solve size-20 puzzles, the optimizer learns moves that work on size-20 instances. It overfits to size-20. MoH trains on sizes 20, 50, 100, 200 all at once, so the LLM learns moves that work on all sizes, not just one. That is generalization.
Cross-size generalization is the metric: train on {20,50,100}, test on 200. Hand-coded optimizers fail; MoH keeps working because the meta-optimizer discovered size-invariant strategy patterns.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: optimizers that learn to adapt
paras: Here is the causal chain. You start by giving the LLM a seed meta-optimizer (a simple hand-coded optimizer recipe, like crossover-then-mutate). But instead of using it directly, the LLM learns to modify it. In iteration 1, the LLM reads the seed recipe, sees the puzzle details (TSP with 20 cities), and generates a new optimizer idea in English: maybe 'select the two most different solutions and combine them'. That becomes optimizer code.

The new optimizer runs on the puzzle, generates solutions, and scores them. If the solutions are good, the LLM learns that this idea was smart. If bad, it learns to discard it. After many iterations on many puzzle types, the LLM has explored a wide space of strategies (crossover, mutation, selection, greedy-insertion, swapping pairs, etc.) and learned which ones generalize.

The key is multi-task training: you train on TSP size-20, TSP size-50, bin packing, vehicle routing, all at once. The LLM cannot overfit to size-20 because half the problems are different sizes or types. It is forced to learn strategies that work universally. So when it faces a new size (200) or new domain, it already understands what works across diversity.

In contrast, a hand-coded optimizer is locked in: it was designed for size-20 TSP, so it breaks on size-200. An LLM that learned only on size-20 also fails. But an LLM trained on sizes 20-50-100-200 discovers size-agnostic principles, so it generalizes.

stages.s: Problem type and size, library of past strategies
LLM proposes a new optimizer idea in English
Convert idea to executable code and run it
Score the solutions the code produced
Measure score, update LLM weights to favor ideas that helped across all problem types
Meta-optimizer that writes good optimizer code for any puzzle type

math.h2: The learning equation: reward the meta-optimizer
math.words: reward_t equals sum_i (solution_quality_i minus baseline_quality) times (did_idea_work) times weight_for_problem_type_i, where the meta-optimizer learns to propose ideas that maximize this reward across all problem types at once
symbols: reward signal to the LLM meta-optimizer at iteration t
index of a problem type (TSP, bin packing, vehicle routing, ...)
the j-th optimizer code generated by the LLM at iteration t
quality (how good the solutions are) when running optimizer I_t^j on problem type i
quality of a standard reference solution (e.g., nearest-neighbor)
weight for problem type i, ensuring equal importance across tasks during multi-task learning

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Iteration t, LLM proposes optimizer idea: 'select top-2 solutions and recombine'.
This optimizer runs on TSP-20 (problem i=1): produces solutions, quality Q_1 = 92. Baseline 85. Gain: 92 - 85 = 7.
Same optimizer on bin packing (problem i=2): quality Q_2 = 84. Baseline 81. Gain: 84 - 81 = 3.
Same optimizer on TSP-100 (problem i=3): quality Q_3 = 55. Baseline 70. Gain: 55 - 70 = -15 (it failed on bigger puzzles).
Reward = (7 * 1) + (3 * 1) + (-15 * 1) = -5. The LLM learns this idea generalizes poorly (great on small TSP, terrible on large TSP), so it down-weights this proposal and tries others.
After 100 iterations, the LLM has learned which ideas have positive reward across all problem types: strategies that work everywhere, not just on one problem type or size.

math.note: The meta-optimizer maximizes reward by proposing ideas that help on every problem type, not just one, forcing it to learn generalizable strategies.

bars.h2: Generalization: hand-coded optimizer vs. learned meta-optimizer

charts.title: Hand-coded optimizer
charts.note: Optimized for small TSP; collapses on larger or different puzzles.

charts.title: MoH meta-optimizer
charts.note: Trained on mix of sizes and types; maintains performance on new puzzles.

items.html: The LLM generates English text that sounds like an algorithm but is vague or circular (e.g., 'pick the best solutions'—best by what measure?). The fix: curate the prompt to ask for specific, executable steps, and have a parser check for syntactic completeness before running the code.

items.b: Overfitting to the training problem set.
items.html: If you train on only TSP and bin packing, the LLM learns TSP-and-bin-packing-specific strategies. It fails on vehicle routing. The fix: train on a diverse set of problem types from the start.

Each LLM-generated optimizer takes time to run. Training the meta-optimizer means generating hundreds of candidate optimizers and running each on many problem instances. This is expensive. The fix: use a small seed population and only run new candidates on a subset of problems each round.

Multi-task training across diverse problem sizes and types, executable code generation with validation, and a clear reward signal (quality minus baseline) ensure the meta-optimizer learns strategies that generalize.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small traveling salesman solver. Start with a hand-coded optimizer (e.g., nearest-neighbor insertion followed by random swaps). Train it on TSP with 20 cities. Measure its accuracy on sizes 20, 50, 100.

Then implement a meta-optimizer: an LLM that reads the problem size and past solution quality, and proposes one mutation to the optimizer code. Train this meta-optimizer on sizes 20, 30, 50, and 70 (a diverse set). For each proposal, run the mutated optimizer, record the solution quality.

After 50 iterations, measure the meta-learned optimizer on size 100 (unseen). The goal is clear: the meta-learned optimizer should maintain or exceed accuracy on size 100, while the hand-coded one tanks.
demo.closing: The demo succeeds if the meta-learned optimizer's generalization failure is <10 percentage points, while the hand-coded optimizer's is >30 points.
